newsitem.title: USA: U.S. kicks off effort to increase seat belt use.
newsitem.headline: U.S. kicks off effort to increase seat belt use.

text.p: The Clinton administration Wednesday set a goal of boosting auto seat belt use to 85 percent by the year 2000, a move it said would save 4,000 lives a year and prevent more than 100,000 injuries.
Transportation Secretary Rodney Slater, opening the seat belt campaign, said that last year more than 40,000 people died on American roads, and another 3.4 million were injured.
"Yet," he said, "nearly a third of all Americans -- and an astonishing 40 percent of children -- don't use their seat belts today."
He said "seat belts are the number one way to save lives, and that's why we want everyone to buckle up for life."
The effort to increase seat belt use was joined by five former transportation secretaries and a broad coalition of safety and business groups.
Highway officials say records show that seat belts, the primary rider protection, save about 9,500 lives a year.

They said some of the nearly 2,000 people that have died because of rapidly inflating air bags could have been saved if adults had been properly buckled up and children riding in the rear seat in a proper safety restraint.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has now allowed car-makers to reduce the inflation rate of airbags -- which now inflate at up to 200 miles an hour.

Officials said seat belt use in America had increased from 14 percent 15 years ago, but had risen little recently, although six states top 80 percent. They are California, Hawaii, New Mexico, North Carolina, Oregon and Washington.
The NHTSA's figures show that an estimated 68 percent of Americans currently use seat belts, saving 9,529 lives a year.
In many industrialized countries, the department said, seat belt use exceeds 85 percent. In Australia, Germany and Canada, use exceeds 90 percent.
Also on Wednesday, President Clinton issued an executive order requiring federal employees to wear seat belts while in a vehicle on official business.
He also ordered that occupants of cars on national park and military base roads be required to use seat belts and that children be buckled in proper child restraints.

Last month, Clinton proposed $124 million in grants to states to improve car occupant protection and more than $1 billion in flexible safety funds that states could use for seat belt enforcement and education.
